Advanced Convolutional Neural Network Framework for Automated Medical Image Diagnosis¶

Introduction¶

The speedy spread of COVID-19 a respiratory diseases has the need for fast and precise diagnostic tools.Imaging of Chest X-ray is the most broadly used and budget-friendly methods for detecting lung abnormalities, including COVID-19 and pneumonia. On the other hand, Expert interpretation of X-ray images can be Time-intensive and may be susceptible to human error , especially during large-scale outbreaks.

Advanceing in deep learning, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have achieved notable results in classification of medical image tasks. These models can without manual intervention learn from medical images the salient features , reducing reliance on handcrafted features and expert intervention. In this project, based on deep learning approach is built so that we can grouping images of chest X-ray into three categories: COVID-19, Pneumonia, and Normal.

Our mission of this study is to design, train, and evaluate a CNN-based classification of that system can assist healthcare professionals by providing reliable and automated diagnosis support. Additionally, multiple controlled experiments are conducted by modifying one parameter at a time to analyze the effect of hyperparameters on model performance.

Problem Statement / Business Problem¶

Timely and accurate diagnosis of COVID-19 and pneumonia is crucial for best treatment and controlling disease spread. Methods such as RT-PCR tests the traditional diagnostic way may consuming a lot of time, expensive, and not always readily available, particularly in resource-constrained environments.

Hospitals and diagnostic centers face challenges such as:

  • High patient volume
  • Limited availability of expert radiologists
  • Delays in diagnosis
  • Class imbalance in medical datasets

The business problem addressed in this project is to develop an automated chest X-ray classification system that can reliably differentiate between COVID-19, pneumonia, and normal cases. Such a system can support clinical decision-making, reduce diagnostic workload, improve screening efficiency, and provide faster preliminary assessments in healthcare settings.

Datset link: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/prashant268/chest-xray-covid19-pneumonia¶

Objectives of the Study¶

The main objectives of this study are as follows:

  • To analyze and understand the dataset of the chest X-ray having COVID-19, pneumonia, and normal images
  • To enhance generalization of the model data preprocessing and augmentation to be performed
  • To sampling and loss weighting techniques are performed so that we can manage class imbalance
  • For multi-class classification a baseline CNN model designed and implemented .
  • The performance of the model to be checked using metrics such as accuracy, loss, confusion matrix, ROC curves, and precision–recall curves
  • To conduct a series of controlled experiments by modifying one hyperparameter at a time and compare their results
  • To identify model that is performing best configuration based on test performance and validation

Step 10: Baseline CNN Model¶

In [44]:
# Step 10: Baseline CNN Model
class BaselineCNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_classes=3):
        super(BaselineCNN, self).__init__()
        
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(1, 32, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(32, 64, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
        self.conv3 = nn.Conv2d(64, 128, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
        
        self.pool = nn.MaxPool2d(2, 2)
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(0.3)
        
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(128 * 28 * 28, 256)  # assuming input size 224x224
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(256, num_classes)
        
    def forward(self, x):
        x = F.relu(self.conv1(x))
        x = self.pool(x)
        
        x = F.relu(self.conv2(x))
        x = self.pool(x)
        
        x = F.relu(self.conv3(x))
        x = self.pool(x)
        
        x = x.view(x.size(0), -1)  # flatten
        x = self.dropout(x)
        x = F.relu(self.fc1(x))
        x = self.fc2(x)  # no softmax, use CrossEntropyLoss
        
        return x

Step 11: Model Compilation¶

In [45]:
# Step 11: Model Compilation

device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
model = BaselineCNN(num_classes=3).to(device)
print(model)
train_class_counts = list(train_counts.values())
total = sum(train_class_counts)
class_weights = [total/count for count in train_class_counts]
class_weights = torch.FloatTensor(class_weights).to(device)

criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss(weight=class_weights)
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.001)

Step 12: Model Training & Validation Loop¶

In [46]:
# Step 12: Model Training & Validation Loop

def calculate_accuracy(y_pred, y_true):
    _, predicted = torch.max(y_pred, 1)
    correct = (predicted == y_true).sum().item()
    return correct / y_true.size(0)

import time
num_epochs = 10  
best_val_acc = 0.0
save_path = "/kaggle/working/best_model.pth"

train_losses, val_losses = [], []
train_accs, val_accs = [], []

for epoch in range(num_epochs):
    start_time = time.time()
    
    # TRAINING 
    model.train()
    running_loss = 0.0
    running_acc = 0.0
    
    for images, labels in train_loader:
        images, labels = images.to(device), labels.to(device)
        
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        outputs = model(images)
        loss = criterion(outputs, labels)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        
        running_loss += loss.item() * images.size(0)
        running_acc += calculate_accuracy(outputs, labels) * images.size(0)
    
    epoch_train_loss = running_loss / len(train_loader.dataset)
    epoch_train_acc  = running_acc / len(train_loader.dataset)
    
    train_losses.append(epoch_train_loss)
    train_accs.append(epoch_train_acc)
    
    # VALIDATION 
    model.eval()
    val_running_loss = 0.0
    val_running_acc  = 0.0
    
    with torch.no_grad():
        for images, labels in val_loader:
            images, labels = images.to(device), labels.to(device)
            outputs = model(images)
            loss = criterion(outputs, labels)
            
            val_running_loss += loss.item() * images.size(0)
            val_running_acc  += calculate_accuracy(outputs, labels) * images.size(0)
    
    epoch_val_loss = val_running_loss / len(val_loader.dataset)
    epoch_val_acc  = val_running_acc / len(val_loader.dataset)
    
    val_losses.append(epoch_val_loss)
    val_accs.append(epoch_val_acc)
    
    # Save the best model
    if epoch_val_acc > best_val_acc:
        best_val_acc = epoch_val_acc
        torch.save(model.state_dict(), save_path)
    
    end_time = time.time()
    
    print(f"Epoch [{epoch+1}/{num_epochs}] "
          f"Train Loss: {epoch_train_loss:.4f}, Train Acc: {epoch_train_acc:.4f} "
          f"Val Loss: {epoch_val_loss:.4f}, Val Acc: {epoch_val_acc:.4f} "
          f"Time: {(end_time - start_time):.1f}s")

print("Training complete. Best validation accuracy: {:.4f}".format(best_val_acc))

Step 16: ROC & Precision–Recall Curves¶

In [51]:
# Step 16: ROC & Precision–Recall Curves

# Number of classes
n_classes = len(test_dataset.classes)

# Binarize true labels (one-hot)
y_true_bin = label_binarize(all_labels, classes=range(n_classes))

# Get prediction probabilities
model.eval()
all_probs = []

with torch.no_grad():
    for images, _ in test_loader:
        images = images.to(device)
        outputs = model(images)
        probs = torch.softmax(outputs, dim=1)
        all_probs.extend(probs.cpu().numpy())

y_scores = np.array(all_probs)
plt.figure(figsize=(7,6))

for i in range(n_classes):
    fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_true_bin[:, i], y_scores[:, i])
    roc_auc = auc(fpr, tpr)
    
    plt.plot(fpr, tpr, label=f"{test_dataset.classes[i]} (AUC = {roc_auc:.3f})")

plt.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], 'k--')
plt.xlabel("False Positive Rate")
plt.ylabel("True Positive Rate")
plt.title("ROC Curve (Multi-Class)")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

plt.figure(figsize=(7,6))

for i in range(n_classes):
    precision, recall, _ = precision_recall_curve(
        y_true_bin[:, i], y_scores[:, i]
    )
    
    plt.plot(recall, precision, label=test_dataset.classes[i])

plt.xlabel("Recall")
plt.ylabel("Precision")
plt.title("Precision–Recall Curve (Multi-Class)")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

Step 17: Model Prediction Visualization¶

In [52]:
# Step 17: Model Prediction Visualization

#  Class names
class_names = test_dataset.classes
print(class_names)

#  Prediction visualization function

def visualize_predictions(model, dataset, device, num_images=6):
    model.eval()
    
    indices = random.sample(range(len(dataset)), num_images)
    plt.figure(figsize=(15, 8))
    
    for i, idx in enumerate(indices):
        image, label = dataset[idx]
        input_image = image.unsqueeze(0).to(device)
        
        with torch.no_grad():
            output = model(input_image)
            _, pred = torch.max(output, 1)
        
        true_label = class_names[label]
        pred_label = class_names[pred.item()]
        
        img = image.squeeze().cpu().numpy()
        
        plt.subplot(2, 3, i + 1)
        plt.imshow(img, cmap="gray")
        
        color = "green" if true_label == pred_label else "red"
        plt.title(f"True: {true_label}\nPred: {pred_label}", color=color)
        plt.axis("off")
    
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

#Run visualization
visualize_predictions(
    model=model,
    dataset=test_dataset,
    device=device,
    num_images=6
)

['COVID19', 'NORMAL', 'PNEUMONIA']

Results and Discussion¶

This study evaluated a CNN model based for multi-class classification of images of chest X-ray into COVID-19, Normal, and Pneumonia categories. The model was trained using augmentation of data, class imbalance handling, and the Adam optimizer.

The baseline CNN demonstrated stable convergence within 10 epochs, with a consistent decrease in loss and improvement in accuracy across training and validation sets, indicating minimal overfitting. Heatmap visualizations further confirmed balanced learning behavior across epochs.

Class imbalance was effectively addressed using a WeightedRandomSampler and class-weighted loss, improving minority class representation, particularly for COVID-19 cases. Test set evaluation showed high overall accuracy, with strong precision, recall, and F1-scores across all classes. The confusion matrix indicated minimal misclassification, while ROC and Precision–Recall curves confirmed strong discriminative performance.

Ten controlled experiments were conducted by changing one parameter at a time from the best model. Among these, Experiment 8 (additional convolutional layer) achieved the highest validation accuracy, highlighting the benefit of deeper feature extraction. Other modifications such as GELU activation and stronger augmentation also improved performance but did not outperform the best model.

Overall, validating the effectiveness of the result proposed architecture CNN for automated chest X-ray classification.

Conclusion¶

This project successfully developed a CNN-based system for grouping chest X-ray images into COVID-19, Normal, and Pneumonia categories. The model achieved high accuracy through effective preprocessing, class imbalance handling, and systematic experimentation.

Experimental results demonstrated that architectural and hyperparameter changes significantly influenced performance, with the best model showing strong generalization on unseen data. These findings indicate that CNN-based approaches can serve as reliable tools to support automated medical image analysis and assist in early diagnosis of respiratory diseases.

Limitations¶

Despite the promising results, this study has several limitations:

  • The dataset size is limited and sourced from a single public repository, which may affect generalization to real-world clinical settings.
  • The model was evaluated only on static X-ray images without incorporating clinical metadata such as patient history or symptoms.
  • Only CNN-based architectures were explored, while more advanced models such as transformers were not considered.
  • The system lacks explainability mechanisms (e.g., Grad-CAM) to visualize decision-making regions in medical images.
  • No real-time clinical validation or hospital deployment was performed.

Future Scope / Improvements¶

Future work can extend this study in several directions:

  • Transfer learning integration done using pre-trained models such as ResNet, EfficientNet, or DenseNet.
  • Inclusion of explainable AI techniques so improve clinical trust and interpretability.
  • Expansion of the dataset using multi-institutional and real-world clinical data.
  • Development of a web-based or mobile diagnostic system for real-time usage.
  • Exploration of multi-modal learning, combining X-ray images with patient clinical data.
  • Optimization for deployment on edge devices and hospital information systems.
